title: Where the Arm Works Well: Reachable Area, Usable Area and the Joint Limits That Cut Both

questions.question: A task point passes the reach check, so the arm can put its tool there. Is that enough to place the work there?
options: Only if it is on the x axis
No: near the edges of the ring the arm is almost straight or folded, close to a singularity, and can be put there without being moved well
questions.explanation: Reachable is a ring, and usable is a smaller one inside it.

questions.question: The grid gave 2.5129 m^2 for a 0.5 and 0.4 m arm. What was it checked against?
options: The area of the ring, pi times (0.9 squared minus 0.1 squared), which is 2.5133
questions.explanation: A grid is checked against a formula where one exists, before it is trusted where none does.

questions.question: Why does best_manipulability look at both elbows?
options: The second elbow is always better
A limit can rule out one pose and not the other, and a map made from one branch reports holes that are not there
questions.explanation: It keeps the better legal one and returns a negative number only when neither is legal.

questions.question: Demanding half of the best manipulability left 86.6 percent of the reachable area and 0.9 left 43.6. What does that show?
options: A mild demand costs almost nothing and a strict one costs most of the ring
questions.explanation: The demand decides how much floor is usable. The area never grows as the demand rises.

questions.question: A shoulder limited to the top half kept 70 percent of the area, not 50. Why?
options: The second link folds back over the shoulder's own side
questions.explanation: The arm reaches points below the shoulder's line. Measure the area under the real limits and do not estimate it.

questions.question: An elbow that bends only one way lost no reachable or usable area. Why, and what did it lose?
options: The two elbow poses for a point are mirror images
questions.explanation: One is always legal; what is lost is the choice between them, which matters to a path and not to a map. Lesson 13-09 showed why keeping a branch matters along a path.
